draft.title: Science in archaeology
card: Archaeologists study the remains of past people, such as bones, tools and buildings. Science helps them find out how old things are and what they can tell us.
Radiocarbon dating
Living things take in carbon, including a rare form called carbon-14. After death the carbon-14 slowly breaks down, so measuring how much is left shows roughly how old the remains are.
DNA testing
DNA is the material in cells that carries genetic information. Testing DNA from bones can show how people were related to each other and to people today.
Ground-scanning radar
This sends radio waves into the ground and records the echoes. It can show buried walls or graves without digging, so a site is less disturbed.
draft.remember: Science lets archaeologists date and study remains, and radar lets them look underground without digging.

a.q: An archaeologist wants to find out how old a wooden beam from an ancient house is. Which method measures the carbon-14 left in it?
a.why: Wood comes from a living tree, so it took in carbon-14. Measuring how much is left shows its approximate age. DNA testing looks at genetic information, not age from carbon.
a.clue: Think about which method has the word carbon in its name.

b.q: A team thinks walls of an ancient town lie under a farm paddock. The farmer wants the soil left mostly undisturbed. Which method should the team use first?
b.why: Radar can show buried walls from the surface without digging. Radiocarbon dating and DNA testing need a sample of remains, and there is nothing to sample until something is found. Digging the whole paddock would disturb the soil, which is what the farmer wants to avoid.
b.clue: Which method can look underground without digging?
